prompt.en: A trainee tapes a high-voltage supply cabinet interlock closed so the cover can stay open during a test, then plans to probe with both hands. What error must be stopped first?

text.en: An open cabinet automatically removes all shock risk, leaving only RF leakage to consider
Defeating the interlock and using both hands removes important shock protections
The only concern is whether the fuse voltage rating is printed on the holder
Increasing the fuse current rating would make the open-cabinet test safer

explanation.en: A cabinet interlock is there to reduce contact with dangerous voltage when the cover is opened. It must not be defeated, and two-handed probing increases the chance of current crossing the chest.

prompt.en: An indoor antenna test is moved from 1 m away from a marked keep-clear line to 2 m away in the same direction, with the same power and antenna. In the simple free-space model, what happens to power density at that line?

text.en: It falls to about one quarter
It falls to about one half
It stays the same because frequency did not change
It increases because the antenna is farther from the operator

explanation.en: Power density follows the inverse-square relationship in the simple free-space model, so doubling distance reduces it to roughly 1/4.

prompt.en: Which statement is NOT true for reducing RF exposure around indoor, UHF, or directional transmitting antennas?

text.en: Moving people farther from the energized antenna usually improves the safety margin
Reducing power or transmission time can lower exposure
A high-gain main beam should not be aimed into occupied nearby space
A low SWR makes it safe for people to stand close to an energized UHF antenna

explanation.en: Low SWR helps the equipment but does not make close human exposure safe. Distance, power, time, antenna gain, beam direction, and access control still matter.
